# Measurement models

``` r

library(ctsem)
library(ggplot2)
```

A ctsem model has two parts. The **dynamic** part describes how the
latent processes change between observations, and the **measurement**
part describes how an observation relates to the latent state at that
time. This vignette is about the measurement part: how many indicators
load on a process, what kind of variable each indicator is, how to
combine kinds, and what to do when a loading or a residual variance is
not constant.

Everything here uses `backend = 'julia'`. The ordinal, count and
censored types are only available there, and the two backends handle
binary indicators differently, so all the examples use the same backend.

## The measurement equation

At each observed time point the filter has a predicted latent state
$`\eta`$. For every manifest variable $`j`$ observed at that time, ctsem
forms a linear predictor

``` math
\mu_j \;=\; \text{MANIFESTMEANS}_j \;+\; \text{LAMBDA}_{j\cdot}\, \eta
```

and then applies the observation model set by that variable’s
`manifesttype`:

| `manifesttype` | Variable | Observation model | Residual |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `0` | continuous | $`y_j \sim N(\mu_j,\ \text{MANIFESTVAR})`$ | free |
| `1` | binary, coded 0/1 | $`P(y_j = 1) = \text{logit}^{-1}(\mu_j)`$ | none |
| `2` | ordinal, coded $`1..K`$ | $`P(y_j \le k) = \text{logit}^{-1}(\tau_{jk} - \mu_j)`$ | none |
| `3` | count, non-negative integers | $`y_j \sim \text{Poisson}(e^{\mu_j + e_j})`$, $`e_j \sim N(0, \text{MANIFESTVAR})`$ | free |
| `4` | censored | $`N(\mu_j,\ \text{MANIFESTVAR})`$, observed only inside $`[\,c^-_j, c^+_j\,]`$ | free |

Four things follow from that table.

**Binary and ordinal indicators have no residual variance.** Their
randomness comes from the link function. A residual term added to the
linear predictor would not be identified: under a probit link
$`E_e\,\Phi(\mu_j + e) = \Phi(\mu_j / \sqrt{1 + v})`$ exactly, so such a
term is absorbed into the loadings and thresholds, and under the
logistic link the same holds approximately. Their rows and columns of
`MANIFESTVAR` are fixed to zero, and
[`ctFit()`](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/reference/ctFit.md) fixes
any that were left free.

**The other three types have a residual, with a different meaning in
each.** For a continuous indicator it is the usual measurement error
variance. For a censored indicator it is the variance of the Gaussian
that is observed only inside the limits. For a count it is a
*dispersion*, a Gaussian term added to the log rate, which makes the
observation Poisson-lognormal. A Poisson’s variance equals its mean,
which is why the dispersion is identified. It shifts the mean by
$`v/2`$, which `MANIFESTMEANS` absorbs, and multiplies the variance by a
factor nothing else in the model can produce. It is the only parameter
in a ctsem model that changes a count’s variance-to-mean ratio. If it is
left out, `DIFFUSION` absorbs any overdispersion, and `DIFFUSION` is
usually a parameter of interest. For counts and censored indicators only
the diagonal is used. Each is scored on its own, so it cannot have
correlated measurement error, and
[`ctFit()`](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/reference/ctFit.md) stops
with an error if an off-diagonal entry is not zero.

**The scale of the latent process has to be fixed somewhere.** With a
Gaussian indicator you can fix a loading or fix `DIFFUSION`. With only
binary or ordinal indicators there is no residual variance to trade
against, so a loading and the process scale describe the same quantity.
Fix the loadings and let `DIFFUSION` carry the scale.

**Location works the same way.** `CINT` and `T0MEANS` set the level of
the process, and each indicator’s `MANIFESTMEANS` sets the level of that
indicator relative to it. By default ctsem fixes `CINT` and `T0MEANS` to
zero and frees `MANIFESTMEANS`, and the examples below, ordinal ones
included, do the same. An ordinal indicator’s thresholds are also
locations, so one of them is redundant: adding a constant to $`\mu_j`$
and to every $`\tau_{jk}`$ leaves the cumulative logit unchanged. ctsem
fixes $`\tau_{j1}`$ at zero, so the location of an ordinal indicator is
in its `MANIFESTMEANS`, as for other indicators, and `THRESHOLDS`
estimates the K-2 gaps between successive thresholds. This lets
`MANIFESTMEANS` be `indvarying`, so that one random effect shifts all of
an indicator’s category boundaries together, which is what a person
answering higher in general means. A random effect on the thresholds
would need one effect for each boundary.

## One indicator or many

A univariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, measured by three indicators at
each occasion with loadings 1, 0.8 and 1.2:

``` r

set.seed(3)
genmulti <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 1, n.manifest = 3,
  manifestNames = c('y1', 'y2', 'y3'), latentNames = 'eta1',
  LAMBDA = matrix(c(1, 0.8, 1.2), 3, 1),
  DRIFT = matrix(-0.4), DIFFUSION = matrix(1.5), T0VAR = matrix(1.7),
  T0MEANS = matrix(0), CINT = matrix(0),
  MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(c(0, 0.5, -0.5), 3, 1),
  MANIFESTVAR = diag(0.8, 3), Tpoints = 10)

dmulti <- data.frame(ctGenerate(genmulti, n = 50, Tpoints = 10,
  backend = 'julia'))
head(dmulti, 3)
#>   id time        y1         y2        y3
#> 1  1    0 -3.347169 -1.8190194 -2.395708
#> 2  1    1 -1.309557 -0.5163224 -2.078168
#> 3  1    2 -1.175804  0.1784173 -1.663167
```

### A single indicator

With one indicator per process the loading cannot be estimated, and is
fixed, by convention to 1. The measurement error can still be estimated.
In a continuous time model, measurement error and process noise have
different effects across time intervals, so `MANIFESTVAR` and
`DIFFUSION` are separately identified.

``` r

msingle <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 1, n.manifest = 1,
  manifestNames = 'y1', latentNames = 'eta1', LAMBDA = matrix(1),
  CINT = matrix(0), T0MEANS = matrix(0))
msingle$pars$indvarying <- FALSE

fsingle <- ctFit(dmulti, msingle, backend = 'julia', cores = 2)
summary(fsingle)$popmeans
#>              mean    sd   2.5%    50%  97.5%   mode
#> drift_eta1 -0.331 0.095 -0.548 -0.317 -0.183 -0.316
#> diff_eta1   1.351 0.226  0.955  1.333  1.830  1.329
#> mvary1      0.973 0.138  0.732  0.960  1.271  0.969
#> mm_y1       0.056 0.163 -0.255  0.060  0.379  0.060
#> T0var_eta1  1.669 0.240  1.237  1.656  2.196  1.645
```

### Three indicators

Freeing the other two loadings, with the first fixed at 1, makes `eta1`
a common factor. The latent process then has the scale of the first
indicator:

``` r

mmulti <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 1, n.manifest = 3,
  manifestNames = c('y1', 'y2', 'y3'), latentNames = 'eta1',
  LAMBDA = matrix(c(1, 'lambda_y2', 'lambda_y3'), 3, 1),
  CINT = matrix(0), T0MEANS = matrix(0))
mmulti$pars$indvarying <- FALSE

fmulti <- ctFit(dmulti, mmulti, backend = 'julia', cores = 2)
summary(fmulti)$popmeans
#>              mean    sd   2.5%    50%  97.5%   mode
#> lambda_y2   0.795 0.027  0.741  0.794  0.847  0.794
#> lambda_y3   1.193 0.035  1.131  1.192  1.262  1.192
#> drift_eta1 -0.417 0.061 -0.553 -0.413 -0.310 -0.410
#> diff_eta1   1.592 0.082  1.443  1.590  1.762  1.592
#> mvary1      0.799 0.037  0.728  0.798  0.872  0.798
#> mvary2      0.785 0.032  0.725  0.785  0.849  0.783
#> mvary3      0.755 0.046  0.669  0.754  0.851  0.755
#> mm_y1       0.069 0.155 -0.225  0.066  0.364  0.068
#> mm_y2       0.615 0.125  0.369  0.612  0.856  0.614
#> mm_y3      -0.419 0.184 -0.764 -0.416 -0.066 -0.418
#> T0var_eta1  1.752 0.193  1.391  1.749  2.137  1.749
```

The loadings come back near their generating values, and the dynamic
parameters are estimated more precisely than from one indicator:

``` r

s1 <- summary(fsingle)$popmeans
s3 <- summary(fmulti)$popmeans
pars <- c('drift_eta1', 'diff_eta1')
data.frame(
  parameter = pars,
  truth = c(-0.4, 1.5),
  single = s1[pars, 'mean'], single_se = s1[pars, 'sd'],
  three = s3[pars, 'mean'], three_se = s3[pars, 'sd'],
  row.names = NULL)
#>    parameter truth single single_se  three three_se
#> 1 drift_eta1  -0.4 -0.331     0.095 -0.417    0.061
#> 2  diff_eta1   1.5  1.351     0.226  1.592    0.082
```

> **Fixing the scale, and starting values**
>
> Fixing `LAMBDA[1,1]` is one way to set the scale. Fixing `DIFFUSION`
> to 1 and freeing all three loadings fits the same model, and reports
> the loadings on the scale of the process instead of the scale of `y1`.
>
> The two are equivalent in principle, but the optimiser can end in
> different places. By default `ctFit` takes starting values for the
> variance parameters from the data (`optimcontrol$datastart`). This
> avoids a local optimum in which the latent variance collapses to zero,
> all of the signal is treated as measurement error, and the loadings
> run off to large values. Some models still lie near the boundary
> between two optima, where the small random variation ctsem adds to the
> starting values decides which one the fit reaches. If a fit reports
> non-convergence, or gives implausible loadings, run it again, and
> compare with `DIFFUSION`-anchored scaling or with explicit `inits`.

## The five indicator types

To see each type on its own, the next example generates one latent
trajectory and measures it in five ways. The process is generated with a
near-zero measurement variance, so that its single manifest variable is
the latent state, from which the indicators below are built:

``` r

set.seed(5)
nsub <- 80; nobs <- 10
process <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 1, n.manifest = 1,
  manifestNames = 'eta', latentNames = 'eta1', LAMBDA = matrix(1),
  DRIFT = matrix(-0.4), DIFFUSION = matrix(1), T0VAR = matrix(1.12),
  T0MEANS = matrix(0), CINT = matrix(0), MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(0),
  MANIFESTVAR = matrix(1e-6), Tpoints = nobs)

d <- data.frame(ctGenerate(process, n = nsub, Tpoints = nobs,
  backend = 'r'))
eta <- d$eta
```

Two indicators of each kind, built by applying each row of the table
above by hand, so that the link in the simulation is the one in the
model:

``` r

invlogit <- function(x) 1 / (1 + exp(-x))
ordinaldraw <- function(mu, tau) {          # cumulative logit
  cum <- sapply(tau, function(k) invlogit(k - mu))
  p <- cbind(cum, 1)
  p <- cbind(p[, 1, drop = FALSE], t(apply(p, 1, diff)))
  apply(p, 1, function(pr) sample.int(length(pr), 1, prob = pmax(pr, 0)))
}
tau <- c(-1, 0, 1)                          # four categories

d$y1 <- 0.0 + eta + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 0.6)              # 0 continuous
d$y2 <- 0.5 + eta + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 0.6)
d$b1 <- rbinom(nrow(d), 1, invlogit(-0.4 + eta))        # 1 binary
d$b2 <- rbinom(nrow(d), 1, invlogit( 0.4 + eta))
d$o1 <- ordinaldraw(eta, tau)                           # 2 ordinal
d$o2 <- ordinaldraw(eta, tau)
disp <- 0.3                                 # count dispersion, on the log rate
d$c1 <- rpois(nrow(d),                                  # 3 count
  exp(1.4 + 0.5 * eta + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, disp)))
d$c2 <- rpois(nrow(d), exp(1.2 + 0.5 * eta + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, disp)))
d$x1 <- pmin(pmax(2.0 + eta + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 0.5), 0), 4)   # 4 censored
d$x2 <- pmin(pmax(1.8 + eta + rnorm(nrow(d), 0, 0.5), 0), 4)

d$eta <- NULL
head(d, 3)
#>   id time           y1          y2 b1 b2 o1 o2 c1 c2        x1        x2
#> 1  1    0 -1.426062341  0.59163773  0  0  2  3  4  1 0.6966535 0.5905002
#> 2  1    1  1.752632464  0.03085567  1  1  2  4  5  3 2.3802010 1.5137950
#> 3  1    2  0.006634949 -0.84232851  1  0  2  4  1  5 0.9411608 1.0590349
```

One subject, seen through all five instruments at once:

``` r

shown <- c('y1', 'b1', 'o1', 'c1', 'x1')
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(shown, function(v)
  data.frame(time = d$time[d$id == 2], value = d[[v]][d$id == 2],
    indicator = v)))
long$indicator <- factor(long$indicator, levels = shown,
  labels = c('y1 continuous', 'b1 binary', 'o1 ordinal', 'c1 count',
    'x1 censored [0,4]'))

ggplot(long, aes(time, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = 'grey60') + geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~indicator, scales = 'free_y', ncol = 2) +
  theme_bw() + labs(x = 'time', y = NULL)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

### Specifying each type

`manifesttype` is a vector with one entry per manifest variable. Two of
the types need further information, because
[`ctModel()`](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/reference/ctModel.md)
does not see the data:

- **ordinal** needs `ncategories`, so that the right number of
  thresholds can be created.
  [`ctGenerate()`](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/reference/ctGenerate.md)
  needs it too.
- **censored** needs `censormin` and `censormax`. These are known
  constants, the floor and ceiling of the instrument, which the data
  cannot estimate. For a variable censored on one side only, leave the
  other limit infinite.

A helper function, since the five models below differ only in their
columns:

``` r

buildmodel <- function(names, type, lambda = 1, ncat = 0,
  cmin = -Inf, cmax = Inf) {
  n <- length(names)
  # binary and ordinal are the two types with no residual of any kind
  mvar <- diag(0, n)
  if (type %in% c(0, 3, 4)) diag(mvar) <- paste0('mvar_', names)
  m <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 1, n.manifest = n,
    manifestNames = names, latentNames = 'eta1',
    manifesttype = rep(type, n), ncategories = rep(ncat, n),
    censormin = rep(cmin, n), censormax = rep(cmax, n),
    LAMBDA = matrix(lambda, n, 1),
    MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(paste0('mm_', names), n, 1), MANIFESTVAR = mvar,
    CINT = matrix(0), T0MEANS = matrix(0))
  m$pars$indvarying <- FALSE
  m
}

models <- list(
  continuous = buildmodel(c('y1', 'y2'), 0),
  binary     = buildmodel(c('b1', 'b2'), 1),
  ordinal    = buildmodel(c('o1', 'o2'), 2, ncat = 4),
  count      = buildmodel(c('c1', 'c2'), 3, lambda = 0.5),
  censored   = buildmodel(c('x1', 'x2'), 4, cmin = 0, cmax = 4))
```

All of these models fix their loadings, so that the latent scale is set
the same way in all five and the dynamic estimates below can be compared
directly.

The count loadings are fixed at 0.5. A count’s loading sets how far its
*log* rate moves as the process moves, and the exponential turns a wide
latent range into a very skewed observation. The filter uses a Gaussian
approximation to the state, which works well for a Poisson update only
while the rate stays in a moderate range. With a loading of 1 on this
process the log rates span about seven units (rates from 0.05 to 50),
and in simulations `DRIFT` and `DIFFUSION` were then clearly
underestimated. Halving the loading halves the range of the log rate,
and the count estimates below are as accurate as the others. If your
counts vary over orders of magnitude, treat their dynamic estimates with
caution.

The count models also estimate a `MANIFESTVAR` diagonal, which for a
count is the dispersion on the log rate, making the observation
Poisson-lognormal. The counts above were generated with a dispersion of
0.3. It is worth freeing for real counts, because otherwise `DIFFUSION`
absorbs any overdispersion.

### The same process, through five instruments

``` r

fits <- lapply(models, function(m) ctFit(d, m, backend = 'julia', cores = 2))

pull <- function(f, p, what) summary(f)$popmeans[p, what]
data.frame(
  type = names(fits),
  drift = sapply(fits, pull, 'drift_eta1', 'mean'),
  drift_se = sapply(fits, pull, 'drift_eta1', 'sd'),
  diffusion = sapply(fits, pull, 'diff_eta1', 'mean'),
  diffusion_se = sapply(fits, pull, 'diff_eta1', 'sd'),
  row.names = NULL)
#>         type  drift drift_se diffusion diffusion_se
#> 1 continuous -0.444    0.052     1.054        0.049
#> 2     binary -0.287    0.117     0.694        0.222
#> 3    ordinal -0.345    0.109     0.890        0.187
#> 4      count -0.356    0.061     0.966        0.082
#> 5   censored -0.436    0.051     1.048        0.045
```

Every row of the table estimates the same two generating values,
$`-0.4`$ and $`1`$, from the same latent trajectory, and every row is
within one and a half standard errors of them. The instruments differ in
how much information about the trajectory they carry, which shows in the
standard errors. Two binary items per occasion carry little information
about a continuous state, and their standard errors are about twice as
large, while the continuous, censored and count pairs each estimate
`DRIFT` with a standard error of 0.05 to 0.06.

The parameters specific to each type are in the same summary. An ordinal
indicator’s location is in `MANIFESTMEANS`. `THRESHOLDS` holds the first
threshold, fixed at zero and not reported, and then the **gap** to each
later threshold, which keeps them in order. A four category variable
therefore has one mean and two gaps:

``` r

thr <- summary(fits$ordinal)$popmeans
gaps <- grep('threshold_o1', rownames(thr), value = TRUE)
thr[c('mm_o1', gaps), c('mean', 'sd')]
#>                 mean    sd
#> mm_o1          0.939 0.117
#> threshold_o1_2 0.997 0.079
#> threshold_o1_3 0.950 0.077

# cumulate the gaps from the pinned zero, then subtract the mean, to read the
# thresholds on the latent scale
cumsum(c(0, thr[gaps, 'mean'])) - thr['mm_o1', 'mean']     # against c(-1, 0, 1)
#> [1] -0.939  0.058  1.008
```

A censored indicator’s residual standard deviation has its usual
meaning. The model estimates it from the uncensored part of the scale,
and treats a value at a limit as the probability of being at or beyond
that limit:

``` r

summary(fits$censored)$popmeans[c('mvar_x1', 'mvar_x2', 'mm_x1', 'mm_x2'),
  c('mean', 'sd')]
#>          mean    sd
#> mvar_x1 0.486 0.027
#> mvar_x2 0.501 0.026
#> mm_x1   2.080 0.074
#> mm_x2   1.901 0.076
mean(d$x1 %in% c(0, 4))     # proportion of x1 observations at a limit
#> [1] 0.10375
```

## Combining types

### Several types on one latent

Indicators of different types can load on the same process. Each
contributes its own likelihood term for the same predicted state, and
the filter’s update at that time uses all of them:

``` r

mixednames <- c('y1', 'b1', 'o1', 'c1', 'x1')
mvar <- diag(0, 5)
mvar[1, 1] <- 'mvar_y1'      # measurement error
mvar[4, 4] <- 'mvar_c1'      # the count's dispersion
mvar[5, 5] <- 'mvar_x1'      # the scale inside the censoring limits

mmixed <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 1, n.manifest = 5,
  manifestNames = mixednames, latentNames = 'eta1',
  manifesttype = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4),
  ncategories   = c(0, 0, 4, 0, 0),
  censormin     = c(-Inf, -Inf, -Inf, -Inf, 0),
  censormax     = c( Inf,  Inf,  Inf,  Inf, 4),
  LAMBDA = matrix(c(1, 1, 1, 0.5, 1), 5, 1),   # the count as generated
  MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(paste0('mm_', mixednames), 5, 1),
  MANIFESTVAR = mvar, CINT = matrix(0), T0MEANS = matrix(0))
mmixed$pars$indvarying <- FALSE

fmixed <- ctFit(d, mmixed, backend = 'julia', cores = 2)
summary(fmixed)$popmeans
#>                  mean    sd   2.5%    50%  97.5%   mode
#> drift_eta1     -0.450 0.049 -0.553 -0.446 -0.360 -0.449
#> diff_eta1       1.034 0.046  0.948  1.031  1.122  1.035
#> mvar_y1         0.622 0.022  0.578  0.622  0.665  0.621
#> mvar_c1         0.319 0.028  0.268  0.318  0.377  0.319
#> mvar_x1         0.496 0.024  0.451  0.496  0.542  0.495
#> mm_y1           0.129 0.079 -0.024  0.130  0.286  0.128
#> mm_b1          -0.223 0.111 -0.443 -0.223 -0.014 -0.222
#> mm_o1           0.942 0.110  0.715  0.943  1.163  0.945
#> mm_c1           1.462 0.043  1.375  1.463  1.546  1.462
#> mm_x1           2.082 0.078  1.928  2.083  2.240  2.082
#> T0var_eta1      1.174 0.098  0.995  1.170  1.368  1.175
#> threshold_o1_2  1.006 0.074  0.862  1.003  1.158  1.004
#> threshold_o1_3  0.952 0.072  0.820  0.947  1.098  0.952
```

One indicator of each kind estimates the process about as precisely as
the best pair of one kind above, and about twice as precisely as the
binary or ordinal pairs, with the thresholds, the three `MANIFESTVAR`
entries and five intercepts estimated as well. It is worth using all the
indicators you have, whatever their kind.

### Several types on different latents

More often, different types measure different things. An ordinal
questionnaire item and a binary event indicator might measure one
construct, and a count, a censored scale score and a continuous variable
another, with the question being how the two constructs affect each
other. That is a two-process model with a block structured `LAMBDA`.

``` r

set.seed(11)
twonames <- c('o1', 'b1', 'c1', 'x1', 'y1')
lambda2 <- matrix(0, 5, 2)
lambda2[1:2, 1] <- 1     # ordinal and binary measure eta1
lambda2[3:5, 2] <- 1     # count, censored and continuous measure eta2

genvar <- diag(0, 5)
genvar[3, 3] <- 0.3      # the count's dispersion, on its log rate
genvar[4, 4] <- 0.4
genvar[5, 5] <- 0.6
gen2 <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 2, n.manifest = 5,
  manifestNames = twonames, latentNames = c('eta1', 'eta2'),
  manifesttype = c(2, 1, 3, 4, 0), ncategories = c(4, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  censormin = c(-Inf, -Inf, -Inf, 0, -Inf),
  censormax = c(Inf, Inf, Inf, 4, Inf),
  LAMBDA = lambda2,
  DRIFT = matrix(c(-0.4, 0.25, -0.15, -0.7), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE),
  DIFFUSION = diag(0.8, 2), T0VAR = diag(1, 2), T0MEANS = matrix(0, 2, 1),
  CINT = matrix(0, 2, 1),
  MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(c(1, -0.4, 0.5, 2.0, 0.3), 5, 1),
  MANIFESTVAR = genvar, Tpoints = 10)

# The first threshold is pinned at zero and the rest are gaps, so thresholds of
# -1, 0 and 1 are a manifest mean of 1 with both gaps at 1.
gen2$pars$value[gen2$pars$matrix %in% 'THRESHOLDS' & gen2$pars$col > 1] <- 1

d2 <- data.frame(ctGenerate(gen2, n = 60, Tpoints = 10,
  backend = 'julia'))
head(d2, 3)
#>   id time o1 b1 c1       x1         y1
#> 1  1    0  1  0  7 2.183019  0.5605175
#> 2  1    1  1  0  1 1.688552 -1.3622011
#> 3  1    2  2  0  1 1.867846  0.3068517
```

`ctGenerate(backend = 'julia')` simulates the latent process and draws
each observation from its measurement model given the state, applying
the links above. The R generator simulates a linear Gaussian system
without links, and warns if asked to generate from a model with
non-Gaussian indicators.

The estimation model has the same block structure, with the measurement
parameters free:

``` r

estvar <- diag(0, 5)
estvar[3, 3] <- 'mvar_c1'
estvar[4, 4] <- 'mvar_x1'
estvar[5, 5] <- 'mvar_y1'

m2 <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 2, n.manifest = 5,
  manifestNames = twonames, latentNames = c('eta1', 'eta2'),
  manifesttype = c(2, 1, 3, 4, 0), ncategories = c(4, 0, 0, 0, 0),
  censormin = c(-Inf, -Inf, -Inf, 0, -Inf),
  censormax = c(Inf, Inf, Inf, 4, Inf),
  LAMBDA = lambda2,
  MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(paste0('mm_', twonames), 5, 1),
  MANIFESTVAR = estvar, CINT = matrix(0, 2, 1), T0MEANS = matrix(0, 2, 1))
m2$pars$indvarying <- FALSE

f2 <- ctFit(d2, m2, backend = 'julia', cores = 2)
summary(f2)$popmeans
#>                   mean    sd   2.5%    50%  97.5%   mode
#> drift_eta1      -0.372 0.138 -0.714 -0.350 -0.163 -0.350
#> drift_eta1_eta2  0.441 0.144  0.166  0.441  0.718  0.443
#> drift_eta2_eta1 -0.176 0.065 -0.303 -0.178 -0.049 -0.177
#> drift_eta2      -0.644 0.085 -0.826 -0.634 -0.496 -0.639
#> diff_eta1        0.893 0.229  0.529  0.874  1.403  0.865
#> diff_eta2_eta1  -0.022 0.163 -0.337 -0.019  0.306 -0.026
#> diff_eta2        0.778 0.046  0.692  0.778  0.870  0.778
#> mvar_c1          0.337 0.055  0.240  0.333  0.457  0.332
#> mvar_x1          0.405 0.022  0.363  0.405  0.450  0.404
#> mvar_y1          0.597 0.023  0.555  0.597  0.640  0.597
#> mm_o1            0.924 0.135  0.656  0.925  1.193  0.927
#> mm_b1           -0.734 0.128 -0.976 -0.736 -0.473 -0.736
#> mm_c1            0.524 0.058  0.413  0.524  0.631  0.525
#> mm_x1            2.091 0.046  1.999  2.092  2.178  2.091
#> mm_y1            0.378 0.051  0.277  0.379  0.472  0.381
#> T0var_eta1       1.290 0.303  0.784  1.257  1.909  1.268
#> T0var_eta2_eta1 -0.335 0.206 -0.745 -0.328  0.063 -0.337
#> T0var_eta2       0.811 0.084  0.658  0.809  0.988  0.806
#> threshold_o1_2   1.050 0.093  0.880  1.048  1.231  1.049
#> threshold_o1_3   0.983 0.095  0.807  0.983  1.173  0.982
```

The cross effects are usually the point of such a model, and here they
are estimated from indicators of four different kinds:

``` r

p2 <- summary(f2)$popmeans
drifts <- c('drift_eta1', 'drift_eta1_eta2', 'drift_eta2_eta1', 'drift_eta2')
data.frame(
  effect = c('eta1 on itself', 'eta2 on eta1', 'eta1 on eta2', 'eta2 on itself'),
  truth = c(-0.4, 0.25, -0.15, -0.7),
  estimate = p2[drifts, 'mean'],
  se = p2[drifts, 'sd'],
  row.names = NULL)
#>           effect truth estimate    se
#> 1 eta1 on itself -0.40   -0.372 0.138
#> 2   eta2 on eta1  0.25    0.441 0.144
#> 3   eta1 on eta2 -0.15   -0.176 0.065
#> 4 eta2 on itself -0.70   -0.644 0.085
```

[`ctKalman()`](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/reference/ctPredict.md)
estimates the latent trajectories from mixed indicators as from any
others:

``` r

plot(ctKalman(f2, subjects = 1:2, timestep = .2), kalmanvec = 'etasmooth')
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## State-dependent measurement

A `LAMBDA` or `MANIFESTVAR` cell need not be constant. Writing a latent
process name into the cell makes it an expression evaluated at the
current state, so an instrument can become more or less sensitive, or
noisier, as the process changes.

Free parameters used inside such an expression must be in the `PARS`
matrix, because ctsem looks up the names in an expression among the
`PARS` entries. `PARS` entries are unbounded and not transformed, so the
residual below is written as `exp(...)` to keep the standard deviation
positive.

Data in which the second indicator’s loading rises with the process, and
so does the first indicator’s residual standard deviation:

``` r

set.seed(9)
gensd <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 1, n.manifest = 2,
  manifestNames = c('y1', 'y2'), latentNames = 'eta1',
  LAMBDA = matrix(c(1, '0.9 + 0.35 * eta1'), 2, 1),
  MANIFESTVAR = matrix(c('exp(-0.7 + 0.3 * eta1)', 0,
    0, 0.8), 2, 2),
  DRIFT = matrix(-0.4), DIFFUSION = matrix(1.5), T0VAR = matrix(1.7),
  T0MEANS = matrix(0), CINT = matrix(0),
  MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(c(0, 0.5), 2, 1), Tpoints = 10)

dsd <- data.frame(ctGenerate(gensd, n = 60, Tpoints = 10,
  backend = 'julia'))
head(dsd, 3)
#>   id time        y1         y2
#> 1  1    0 -1.617416  0.1401635
#> 2  1    1 -1.797942 -0.4742866
#> 3  1    2 -1.316891 -0.6378433
```

The estimation model uses the same two expressions, with parameter names
in place of the generating constants:

``` r

msd <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 1, n.manifest = 2,
  manifestNames = c('y1', 'y2'), latentNames = 'eta1',
  LAMBDA = matrix(c(1, 'lam0 + lamslope * eta1'), 2, 1),
  MANIFESTVAR = matrix(c('exp(logsd0 + logsdslope * eta1)', 0,
    0, 'mvar_y2'), 2, 2),
  MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(c(0, 'mm_y2'), 2, 1),
  CINT = matrix(0), T0MEANS = matrix(0),
  PARS = matrix(c('lam0', 'lamslope', 'logsd0', 'logsdslope'), 4, 1))
msd$pars$indvarying <- FALSE

fsd <- ctFit(dsd, msd, backend = 'julia', cores = 2)
summary(fsd)$popmeans
#>              mean    sd  2.5%   50% 97.5%   mode
#> drift_eta1 -0.446    NA    NA    NA    NA -0.443
#> diff_eta1   1.418    NA    NA    NA    NA  1.413
#> mvar_y2     0.779 0.043 0.698 0.777 0.865  0.777
#> mm_y2       0.636 0.051 0.536 0.635 0.735  0.633
#> T0var_eta1  1.816 0.176 1.506 1.806 2.182  1.810
#> lam0        0.829    NA    NA    NA    NA  0.829
#> lamslope    0.321    NA    NA    NA    NA  0.323
#> logsd0     -0.376    NA    NA    NA    NA -0.375
#> logsdslope  0.194    NA    NA    NA    NA  0.195
```

Against the generating values:

``` r

psd <- summary(fsd)$popmeans
sdpars <- c('lam0', 'lamslope', 'logsd0', 'logsdslope')
data.frame(
  parameter = sdpars,
  meaning = c('loading on y2 at eta1 = 0',
    'change in that loading per unit of eta1',
    'log residual sd of y1 at eta1 = 0',
    'change in that log sd per unit of eta1'),
  truth = c(0.9, 0.35, -0.7, 0.3),
  estimate = psd[sdpars, 'mean'],
  row.names = NULL)
#>    parameter                                 meaning truth estimate
#> 1       lam0               loading on y2 at eta1 = 0  0.90    0.829
#> 2   lamslope change in that loading per unit of eta1  0.35    0.321
#> 3     logsd0       log residual sd of y1 at eta1 = 0 -0.70   -0.376
#> 4 logsdslope  change in that log sd per unit of eta1  0.30    0.194
```

[`ctModelIsNonlinear()`](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/reference/ctModelIsNonlinear.md)
reports that such a model has cells that change with the state, so any
summary of it is a reading at one particular state:

``` r

ctModelIsNonlinear(fsd)
#> [1] TRUE
```

A state dependent model is therefore better described by curves than by
single numbers.
[`ctStateDependencePlot()`](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/reference/ctStateDependencePlot.md)
finds the cells that change with the state, by computing every model
matrix over a grid of states, and plots each of them against the
process. This includes cells that depend on the state indirectly,
through a `PARS` entry or a covariance built from a state dependent
cell:

``` r

ctStateDependencePlot(fsd, along = 'eta1', nsamples = 30)
```

![](data:image/png;base64,)

One panel shows the loading on `y2`, rising with `eta1`. The other shows
the residual *variance* of `y1` (`MANIFESTcov`, the covariance the
filter uses), which rises as well. A
[`summary()`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/summary.html) of this model reports
one point from each of these curves.

Only `LAMBDA` and `MANIFESTVAR` depend on the state here, but
`MANIFESTMEANS` can too, and on the dynamic side so can `DRIFT`,
`DIFFUSION` and `CINT`.

## Summary

- `manifesttype` sets the observation model for each indicator: `0`
  continuous, `1` binary, `2` ordinal (with `ncategories`), `3` count,
  `4` censored (with `censormin` and `censormax`). Types `2` to `4` need
  `backend = 'julia'`.
- Continuous, count and censored indicators each have a free
  `MANIFESTVAR` diagonal, which is the measurement error variance, the
  dispersion on the log scale, and the variance inside the limits
  respectively. Binary and ordinal indicators have none, and
  [`ctFit()`](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/reference/ctFit.md)
  fixes theirs to zero.
- An ordinal indicator’s location is its `MANIFESTMEANS`, as for every
  other indicator. `THRESHOLDS` fixes the first threshold at zero and
  estimates the K-2 gaps, so a person level shift of the whole category
  scale is one random effect on the mean.
- Fix the latent scale once, with a fixed loading or a fixed
  `DIFFUSION`. With no Gaussian indicator on a process, fix the
  loadings.
- A count indicator’s loading sets how far its log rate moves. Keep that
  range moderate, because the filter’s Gaussian approximation of a
  Poisson update degrades once the rate varies over orders of magnitude,
  and the dynamic parameters are then underestimated.
- Types can be mixed, on one process or across several.
- A `LAMBDA` or `MANIFESTVAR` cell written as an expression of a latent
  process is evaluated at the current state. Free parameters inside it
  go in `PARS`, and
  [`ctStateDependencePlot()`](https://cdriveraus.github.io/ctsem/reference/ctStateDependencePlot.md)
  shows how the cell changes with the state.
